# Model validation

Generated from `reports/results.json`, `data/processed/backtest_results.parquet` and the cubes.
Bootstrap: 2,000 client-level replicates (41,448 clients, seed 20261004),
95% percentile intervals.

## 1. Absorbing chain and the point of no return

| Bucket | P(eventual CO), DORMANT included [95% CI] | P(eventual pay-off) | Months to resolution [95% CI] | P(eventual CO), X dropped | Months, X dropped |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-29 | 1.2% [1.0% to 1.4%] | 98.8% | 21.1 [20.7, 21.3] | 1.0% | 17.5 |
| 30-59 | 2.6% [2.2% to 3.0%] | 97.4% | 19.3 [18.9, 19.6] | 2.8% | 16.0 |
| 60-89 | 20.2% [17.0% to 23.5%] | 79.8% | 15.5 [14.6, 16.3] | 23.3% | 12.3 |
| 90-119 | 51.4% [45.4% to 57.5%] | 48.6% | 8.7 [7.6, 9.9] | 56.8% | 6.3 |
| 120-149 | 74.9% [68.7% to 80.9%] | 25.1% | 3.5 [2.6, 4.6] | 78.2% | 2.4 |

The point of no return (first bucket where eventual charge-off is more likely than eventual pay-off) is
**90-119** with DORMANT included and **90-119** with X dropped. The same bucket is selected
in 68% and 98% of
bootstrap replicates respectively (other replicates select: 120-149). With DORMANT included, the interval for
P(eventual charge-off) at 90-119 includes 50%, so the cliff between 60-89 and the
90+ buckets is well supported while the exact bucket is not certain.
Including DORMANT lowers P(eventual CO) for severe buckets and lengthens resolution times, because dormant spells
delay resolution and some dormant accounts later pay off.

## 2. Out-of-time rolling-origin backtest

Origins -36 to -3 every 3 months with at least
24 months of training transitions; 32 origin x horizon pairs. Training uses only
transitions whose destination month is at or before the origin (enforced by `tests/test_markov.py`). Target:
closed-cohort run-off of accounts in DORMANT or 1-29 to 120-149 at the origin. Primary comparison: full-cohort
forecast against the state shares of cohort members observed at the target month (mean missing share
8.9%); the observed-subset forecast is stored as the `markov_observed` sensitivity.
Baselines: persistence (every account stays in its origin state) and static mix (the portfolio's state mix at the
origin, all eight states, copied forward). The in-sample oracle uses the full-window matrix and is an upper bound only.

| Horizon | Origins | Latest origin | Markov MAE latest (pp) [95% CI] | Persistence MAE | Static-mix MAE | Skill vs persistence | Skill vs static mix | Mean MAE pooled / rolling / MOB | Wins vs static mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3M | 12 | -3 | 2.65 [2.49, 2.84] | 5.31 | 11.26 | 0.50 [0.47, 0.53] | 0.76 [0.75, 0.78] | 0.77 / 0.62 / 0.52 | 12 of 12 |
| 6M | 11 | -6 | 2.81 [2.63, 3.01] | 7.91 | 8.13 | 0.65 [0.62, 0.67] | 0.65 [0.63, 0.68] | 1.37 / 1.17 / 0.73 | 11 of 11 |
| 12M | 9 | -12 | 2.99 [2.80, 3.19] | 11.79 | 3.49 | 0.75 [0.73, 0.76] | 0.14 [0.12, 0.17] | 1.81 / 1.66 / 1.18 | 8 of 9 |

- The Markov model beats persistence at every horizon by a wide margin; persistence ignores pay-off and dormancy.
- Against the static-mix baseline the margin is small: skill 0.14 at the latest 12M origin.
- State-share MAE is dominated by DORMANT, 1-29 and PAID-OFF; per-state errors are on the dashboard.
- Mean absolute charge-off share error at 12M: 0.32 pp.

### Charge-off count calibration

The actual charge-off count falls inside the 95% bootstrap predictive interval in 21 of
32 pairs. At the latest 12M origin the model implies 50.0 charge-offs against
31 observed (interval 34 to 68).
The observed count is outside the interval: the pooled chain over-predicts charge-offs for recent cohorts.

## 3. Is first-order Markov enough?

**Stationarity.** 4 of 6 origin rows reject
homogeneity between the first and second half of the window at 5%. Out-of-time 12M MAE from origin -12:
3.45 pp with the first-half matrix vs 2.99 pp with the expanding matrix.

| FROM_STATE | chi2 | dof | p_value | n | total_variation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DORMANT | 125.6 | 7 | 5.2e-24 | 55,166 | 0.0484 |
| 1-29 | 754.4 | 7 | 1.3e-158 | 372,573 | 0.025 |
| 30-59 | 52.6 | 6 | 1.4e-09 | 10,737 | 0.0513 |
| 60-89 | 13.5 | 6 | 0.036 | 849 | 0.1238 |
| 90-119 | 9.9 | 7 | 0.19 | 314 | 0.1473 |
| 120-149 | 10.7 | 6 | 0.1 | 218 | 0.1083 |

**MOB bands.** 6 of 6 origin rows reject equal destination
distributions across MOB bands (early 0-6, middle 7-18, mature 19+).

| FROM_STATE | chi2 | dof | p_value | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DORMANT | 1886.5 | 14 | 0 | 55,166 |
| 1-29 | 1960.2 | 14 | 0 | 372,573 |
| 30-59 | 83.2 | 12 | 1e-12 | 10,737 |
| 60-89 | 57.7 | 12 | 6e-08 | 849 |
| 90-119 | 42.1 | 14 | 0.00012 | 314 |
| 120-149 | 51.9 | 12 | 6.4e-07 | 218 |

Band differences (mature minus early) whose 95% interval excludes zero: 2 of
6 key transitions tested. The MOB-conditioned forecast (band matrices applied
in sequence as MOB advances, Dirichlet smoothing tuned on training data only) has mean 12M MAE
1.18 pp against 1.81 pp for the pooled model:
the data favour conditioning on MOB.

**History (Anderson-Goodman).** Does the previous state change P(next | current) for 30+ origins?

| CUR_STATE | chi2 | dof | p_value | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30-59 | 987.2 | 24 | 4.7e-193 | 10,549 |
| 60-89 | 252.4 | 30 | 5.1e-37 | 837 |
| 90-119 | 190.1 | 35 | 3.2e-23 | 308 |
| 120-149 | 121.3 | 24 | 5.8e-15 | 213 |

Chi-square tests on sparse severe rows are approximate; thin rows are flagged on the dashboard.

## 4. Conclusion

The pooled first-order chain is a useful baseline: it beats both naive baselines on state-share error.
It is not sufficient on its own. Transition behaviour differs by MOB band and between the two halves of the
window, and the pooled matrix over-predicts charge-offs at the latest 12M origin.
A MOB-conditioned chain is the better forecaster in this data.
